context: To overcome this limitation, we consider a different parameter that is often much smaller than σ. Specifically, we define ∆ ≥ max1≤i<n |T [i + 1] − T [i]|, which bounds the absolute difference between adjacent characters. This parameter is natural for discretized signals, such as time-series data, where consecutive values change gradually. It is also meaningful in stochastic settings: for a simple symmetric random walk on the integers, we have ∆ = 1, yet √ the maximum value attained over n steps is Θ( n) in expectation [25]. Thus, even when ∆ is constant, the range of values in T can be large. Observe that such a string T can be represented in O(n log ∆) bits by storing T [1] and the successive differences T [i + 1] − T [i]. While standard techniques support constant-time random access within this space, building an index that enables efficient pattern matching remains open. To address this, we consider the following problem: Problem: Differentially Encoded Indexing. Given ∆ ≥ 2 and T [1 . . n], a length-n string of integers such that |T [i + 1] − T [i]| ≤ ∆ for all 1 ≤ i < n, we seek a data structure to answer queries of the following form: Input: A length-m string P [1 . . m] of integers (called a pattern). Output: A reporting query asks to output the set of all occurrences of P in T , that is {i1 , i2 , . . . , iocc } ⊆ [1 . . n] such that P = T [ij . . ij + m) for each j. A counting query asks to return occ, the size of that set. We restrict our attention to ∆ ≥ 2, since even if the maximum difference has absolute value 1, a bound of ∆ ≥ 2 trivially holds. Our main result is summarized in Theorem 1.
